about: Browser TTS batches. Generate each batch as ONE audio file named <id>.mp3/.wav with the voice for its role. Parts are separated by a blank line in 'text'; offline alignment splits each file back into segment parts by these exact texts.
rules: text is verbatim: never edit, add or drop words
one file per batch, named exactly by id
same voice and settings for every batch of a role
roles other than heba/nico are short; they may be merged by the author into one voice per role

voice_roles.heba: Ivy narration and Ivy's own dialogue - the genuine cloned 'heba' voice (NOT the designed 'heba eng')
voice_roles.nico: Nico (segments labelled lion + his quoted lines)

n053#0.evidence: reply to 'Go after him' by Rocco, the only man in the doorway

n081#0.evidence: Sal holds up both hands, cannoli in one

n102#0.evidence: Enzo grabbed my sleeve and told me

n109#0.evidence: 'Nico, in the car, never raised his voice'

n136#0.evidence: 'Theo walked out ... In the car he said'

quotes_kept_with_narrator.ambiguous / not voiced: n098 (Bell's written phone note, read by Ivy) · n110 ('destroyed' is a scare quote) · n113 and n149 (the questioner is not named on the line)

batches.text:
Two shots. That's all it took.

Ten past four that Friday morning, crouched behind my own bumper in a hospital garage, I learned what a life ending sounds like in concrete.

I looked over the hood. A man was sliding down the side of a silver sedan, a gun a foot from his open hand. The man standing over him held a different gun, in his left hand. His right arm was in the plaster splint I had built thirty minutes earlier, in bay fourteen, with my own two hands.

I went back inside. Three days later I married him.

It started at 3:05 that morning, with a man walking into my ER holding his own arm closed. Half the waiting room went quiet for him. Denise at triage half stood up. The security guard found something interesting on his shoes. Everybody knew a rule about this man. Nobody had told me.

Bay fourteen. A clean cut across the inside of his right forearm. Gray eyes. A thin white scar through his left eyebrow.

Knife?" I asked.

Somewhere you need to be?

A couple hundred times. Usually on people who tell me their name.

By 3:40 I had built him a splint of plaster, fingertips to elbow. Six weeks, no gripping. If he grabbed anything hard, that tendon would snap like a rubber band. He set a fold of hundreds on my tray.

There's always a chart." I tucked the money back into his pocket and typed his name while he watched. I said it too hard. He couldn't know why.

Level two, spot 2-14. At 4:08 I found the charger in the cup holder. At 4:10, two shots went off, so close together they sounded like one word. I counted. One, two, three, four. Footsteps. Something heavy hitting a car door. At nine, I looked.

Let me get to him," I said. "I can—

Behind him, in the stairwell, feet were going down fast. Then they stopped. Someone was standing on those stairs, listening, and those stairs were my only way out. I counted his breaths. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten. The next one didn't come. The last time I stood that close to someone dying while other people decided I should stay out of the way, I was fourteen.

At 4:16 I called 911 and my voice came out steady. By 4:31 the silver sedan was gone, and so was the man. The floor smelled like bleach and fake pine. The camera had been down since Tuesday. A young officer told me a car backfiring sounds like a cannon in concrete.

I had a name on my tongue. I didn't say it. I'm not proud of that.

Saturday at eight, a woman in a rain jacket and a man in a navy suit sat on my couch. Special Agent Reyes. Prosecutor Holloway. A city crew had pulled a man out of the Gowanus Canal. Frankie Lombardi. Two gunshot wounds to the chest. Frankie worked for the Vescari family, and also, quietly, for the FBI. That made his murder a federal case, and me its witness.

I told them in order, like presenting a patient. Two shots at 4:10. Nico standing over a man by a silver car, a gun in his left hand, my splint on his right. Notice what I didn't say: that I saw anyone fire. I heard two shots. I saw what came after.

Holloway left a subpoena. Thursday, ten a.m. He offered a new name, a new city, witness protection. I laughed. I had nine months of residency left. I wasn't becoming a dental hygienist in Tucson because a man in a nice suit told me to go back inside.

I'll tell them," I said. "But I'm doing it as myself.

At seven that night I carried groceries up three flights and found my door unlocked and my lamp off. Nico Vescari sat in my mother's armchair in the dark, my splint resting on the arm. My little brother sat beside him, white as paper.

Theo said.

Forty thousand dollars, a betting app, then interest. Theo was crying the way he did at fifteen, when he thought I couldn't hear through the wall.

So someone wants me dead, and it isn't you.

Did you kill that man?

I laughed. "I met you on Friday. You bled on my shoes. Here's my answer." I held up the subpoena. "I'd rather testify.

Sunday, a man in bay seventeen asked for the redheaded doctor. In the supply room the door clicked shut and IV tubing dropped over my head. You get about ten seconds before you pass out. I teach that to students. At five I drove my trauma shears into the back of his hand, and he ran.

A huge man filled the doorway, the quiet one with the crossword. Rocco. "Go after him," I croaked.

batches.text:
That evening I stood by my car with a red line round my throat. I could become someone else in a city I'd never seen, or keep my work and my brother and trust a man I didn't. I was scared of him. I was more scared of a plastic tube. He answered on the first ring.

I have conditions," I said.

His lawyer wrote it down in blue ink. One. I keep my residency, every shift. Two. My own bedroom, with a lock on my side. Three. Theo's debt, gone tonight. Four. No one in his family touches me, including his men. Five. When the case is dead, we divorce. Six. Not one cent of his money.

And seven. You never lie to me.

That's a loophole.

Is it the only reason you want this? If I can't testify, you're safe?

What's the other one?

He held my eyes and said nothing at all. Beside him, Tommy looked at the table. Whatever it was, Tommy knew.

Eleven pages, typed overnight. At the bottom of Nico's section, someone had added a line by hand in big, shaky, left-handed capitals. She will look like she loves me. I initialed it. I read every page twice.

The ring was his grandmother's, a square emerald, far too big. It slid around my finger.

he said.

On the courthouse steps, eight reporters and three cameras. Holloway had been tipped. Nico kissed me, slow and warm, the plaster along my spine. It was for the cameras. For three seconds I forgot to count anything, and I was angry about that all day.

He had put a bolt on my side of the connecting door himself, at six that morning, left-handed. The screws were crooked. I tested it four times. The ring was so loose it kept turning to my palm.

Tuesday, the ER. At work I couldn't wear a ring under gloves, so I'd threaded his grandmother's emerald onto a thin gold chain and tucked it under my scrubs. A wedding ring that lived against my breastbone. Joey, one of Nico's soldiers, rolled in stabbed, lung collapsing. I decompressed him and put in the tube myself while mobsters watched me do it.

he asked. "Not on my shift.

In his jacket I found my whole October. Every shift in blue ballpoint, small neat slanted handwriting I didn't know. And at the bottom, underlined twice: Level 2. Space 2-14.

Joey said the man who sent him drove a car that smelled like anise. Only the hospital had my schedule. Dr. Bell had asked about my shifts that morning, almost casually. I told myself Bell asks everybody everything.

I confronted Bell Thursday evening. He cried. His son Danny was seventeen and sick, and the treatment cost four hundred seventy thousand dollars. A man had asked about my schedule. Bell gave it. I gave him until noon to call the FBI. He asked for one more night. I said yes. I have thought about that yes every day since.

That night I was shaking, and he held me, and he pulled the pen out of my hair with his left hand. I kissed him. He kissed me back. I stopped. No cameras. "That one wasn't for anyone," I said.

he said.

At 6:41 Friday morning, Priya called. Dr. Bell was dead in his Volvo, three spaces from my spot. A note on his phone. Suicide. "Ivy, I'm sorry. I couldn't live with it. Tell Danny I tried.

In three years Bell called me Ivy maybe four times, always when someone had just died. In writing, always Marlowe, even in his last text. The note was a lie, and whoever wrote it didn't know him.

Only four people had known he'd talk to the FBI at noon. Nico. Tommy. Rocco. And Nico's uncle Sal. When I said that name aloud, Nico's eyes dropped to the top drawer of his desk, for as long as it takes to read a clock.

Sunday lunch under the fig. Enzo excused himself and didn't come back. I found him on his bathroom floor, blue, a foil card beside him. Oxycodone, thirty milligrams. I breathed for him. Two sprays of naloxone, three minutes apart. He gasped. I put the card in my cardigan pocket before the paramedics came. I only knew it mattered.

In the ER, Enzo grabbed my sleeve and told me, because he thought he was dying.

He had followed Frankie into the garage and stood half a flight up the stairs, holding his breath. A shoe scraped. Frankie turned, and his gun came up. Enzo fired twice and didn't even decide to. Nico took the gun out of his hand and told him to go.

Enzo was the light jacket on the stairs. He had stopped when he heard me ask for a tube. Then he kept going. I told him what he said in that bay stays with me. I didn't know yet what it would cost.

batches.text:
Then Theo was arrested. Four hundred tablets, taped under the driver's seat of his Civic. Holloway offered a trade: my testimony against Nico, and Theo walks. Nico, in the car, never raised his voice.

I had my own evidence. The sticker on Enzo's card said Lot 4471-B. So did the pills in Theo's car. I cornered the hospital pharmacy director with an old committee letter. Forty-two cards of that lot had been "destroyed" on a form dated September twenty-ninth, co-signed by Dr. Marcus Bell. The tech said nobody counted. The signing doctor carried the bag out himself, past the garage.

Nico's people found the dealer. His supplier was an old man in a gray Lincoln that smelled of licorice.

Monday, Courtroom 6B. Holloway wanted the judge to call it a sham marriage. He called me to the stand and asked about the first week. About the courthouse kiss. And I invited him to ask the real question.

Do you love your husband?

Yes. I love him. And I'd like the record to show he's hearing it for the first time with everyone else.

The judge denied the motion from the bench. She'd seen a great many sham marriages, and none of them sounded like that. In the car, Nico's left hand lay open on the seat, palm up. I put mine in it. At my door he said,

At midnight I couldn't sleep. Holloway had asked me that morning,

Only I, Nico, Mr. Feld and one copy in Nico's top drawer knew how many pages the contract had. Someone inside the house was talking to the government's side. I opened the drawer. Under the paper, a white twist of candy wrapper. It smelled of anise.

At dawn, Danny Bell let me read his father's last letter. Marcus had signed the destruction form and carried the pills to a gray car for cash. Years ago he'd misdiagnosed a patient who turned out to be Brancato's cousin, and Brancato had held it over him ever since. The man in the gray car was old, soft-spoken, nice coat. The letter ended: Ivy, say it. Say all of it. Danny said I could give it to the FBI. I gave Reyes everything except one name. "Somebody else gets to tell you first," I said.

Tuesday, seven p.m. Sal arrived exactly on time with a box of pastry. Nico laid out the notebook, the receipt, the jacket. Sal didn't blink.

he said,

he said.

I broke my own rule and spoke. "I breathed for your nephew for four minutes, Mr. Vescari. On your pills.

Sal looked at his hands, then at his nephew.

I put my phone on the tablecloth and called Agent Reyes on speaker. Sal almost smiled.

A day later I chained a deli receipt and a pack of gum to Paulie Ferraro. I called Reyes first, on purpose. Then Nico.

Paulie confessed. Theo walked out at 12:52. In the car he said,

I'd been so busy keeping him safe that I'd never asked. I asked.

Monday night Lucia found Enzo's room empty. At 11:31 my phone rang. Carmine Brancato. I told everyone before, not after. I texted Reyes. I went.

batches.text:
That evening there was a cream envelope on the hall table. Term Five. Three stapled pages. He'd signed it with his right hand, slowly, like a man writing in a foreign language. I put the papers down and went upstairs.

I didn't knock. "Here's the thing about the divorce," I said. "I haven't asked." I emptied my cardigan pockets onto his bed: Enzo's foil card, the pharmacy form, his note, Bell's envelope, a candy twist. Everything I'd carried through five weeks. I took the pen out of my hair. On page eleven, under his left-handed line, I wrote, She does. And under that: Term six. Nobody in this house is quiet anymore.

April. The lemon trees came out of their burlap.

Lucia said.

Theo has an apartment over a laundromat and comes for Saturday lunch and calls me Iv. Enzo is in a program upstate, a hundred forty-one days clean, writing to his mother on Sundays and to a boy named Anthony who hasn't answered yet. Sal's letters from Cefalù, Lucia burns unread. Danny Bell is back at school; an anonymous donor paid his treatment. When I asked, Nico said,

and smiled. I finish residency in June.

Reyes came to the gate on the first warm Saturday. A motion from Brancato's lawyers had surfaced old files. Nico's father had been an FBI informant for years. Nico would read it in the Post by Friday.

I did not wait. We don't do silence in this house anymore. It's in the contract. I climbed fourteen stairs, counting every one, to tell my husband the truth about his father. Two shots. That's all it took to start all of this. One yes, said out loud, is how it ended.
